frameworkNote: These thinking patterns are drawn from public cognitive behavioral frameworks (Aaron Beck and David Burns). This is educational self-reflection to help you notice your own thoughts, not therapy or any kind of diagnosis.

distortions.name: All-or-Nothing Thinking
distortions.description: You see things in absolute, black-and-white terms. If it is not a total success, you count it as a total failure.
distortions.example: I missed one week at the gym, so I have completely blown my whole fitness plan.
reframePrompts: Where on the scale from 0 to 100 does this actually sit, if you are honest?
What would you tell a friend who described this exact situation to you?
Is 'ruined' really true, or did one part go worse than you wanted?
distortions.reframeTemplate: It is not all-or-nothing. The part that did not go well was ______, and the parts that still stand are ______. A more accurate line is: this was partly hard and partly fine, and I can pick it back up from here.
distortions.citation: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy.

distortions.name: Overgeneralization
distortions.description: You treat a single event as a never-ending pattern, often using words like 'always' or 'never'.
distortions.example: I got turned down for that role. I never get chosen for anything.
reframePrompts: Is this one event, or a genuine pattern with several examples?
Can you name even one time the opposite was true?
What are the specific facts here, without the words 'always' or 'never'?
distortions.reframeTemplate: One thing happened: ______. That is a single event, not a rule about my whole life. A time it went differently was ______, which tells me this is not 'always'.
distortions.citation: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy.

distortions.name: Mental Filter
distortions.description: You lock onto one negative detail and let it color everything, filtering out the rest of the picture.
distortions.example: One person gave critical feedback in the meeting, so the whole presentation was a disaster.
reframePrompts: What are you leaving out of the frame right now?
If you listed everything that happened, how much of it was actually negative?
What would the full picture look like, not just the one detail?
distortions.reframeTemplate: I have been staring at ______ and letting it stand in for everything. Widening the lens, what else was true is ______. The one hard detail is real, and it is not the whole story.
distortions.citation: Beck, A. T. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression.

distortions.name: Discounting the Positive
distortions.description: You dismiss good things as if they do not count, insisting they were luck, easy, or expected.
distortions.example: They only praised my work to be polite. It was not really that good.
reframePrompts: Why does this good thing 'not count' when a bad thing would?
If a peer had done this, would you brush it off the same way?
What are you doing to earn the good outcome that you are refusing to credit?
distortions.reframeTemplate: I am tempted to wave this away as ______, but the honest version is: I did ______, and that counts. Letting the good news land does not make me arrogant, it makes me accurate.
distortions.citation: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy.

distortions.name: Jumping to Conclusions
distortions.description: You decide you know what will happen or what someone thinks, with no real evidence, then treat the guess as fact.
distortions.example: She has not texted back, so she must be annoyed with me.
reframePrompts: What is the actual evidence, versus the story you are filling in?
What are two other explanations that would also fit the facts?
Are you predicting the future or reading a mind here?
distortions.reframeTemplate: I am treating a guess as a fact. The evidence I actually have is ______. An equally likely explanation is ______. Until I know more, I can hold this as a maybe, not a verdict.
distortions.citation: Beck, A. T. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression.

distortions.name: Magnification (Catastrophizing)
distortions.description: You blow the importance of a problem out of proportion, or shrink things down until they seem trivial.
distortions.example: If I mess up this one email, my whole reputation is finished.
reframePrompts: How much will this actually matter in a week? In a year?
What is the realistic worst case, and could you handle it if it happened?
Are you sizing this by the facts, or by how anxious you feel right now?
distortions.reframeTemplate: Right now this feels enormous: ______. Sized realistically, the likely outcome is ______, and even the worst case I could handle by ______. It is a real problem, not a catastrophe.
distortions.citation: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy.

distortions.name: Emotional Reasoning
distortions.description: You take how you feel as proof of how things are. If you feel it, you assume it must be true.
distortions.example: I feel like a fraud, so I must actually be one.
reframePrompts: Is this a feeling, or a fact? They are not the same thing.
What would the evidence say if you set the feeling aside for a moment?
Have you felt this way before about something that turned out fine?
distortions.reframeTemplate: I feel ______, and that feeling is real. But a feeling is not evidence. The facts on the ground say ______. I can feel this way and still act on what is actually true.
distortions.citation: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy.

distortions.name: Should Statements
distortions.description: You beat yourself or others with rigid rules about how things ought to be, and feel guilt, pressure, or resentment when reality does not comply.
distortions.example: I should be further along by now. I should never need help.
reframePrompts: Whose rule is this, and is it one you would actually choose?
What happens to how you feel when you swap 'should' for 'I would like to'?
Is this standard fair, or one you would never hold anyone else to?
distortions.reframeTemplate: The rule running me is: I should ______. Restated as a preference: I would like to ______, and it is okay that I am not there yet. Dropping the whip does not drop the goal.
distortions.citation: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy.

distortions.name: Labeling
distortions.description: You pin a harsh, fixed label on yourself or someone else based on one action, instead of describing the specific behavior.
distortions.example: I forgot the deadline. I am such a loser.
reframePrompts: Are you describing what you did, or slapping a label on who you are?
Would you call a friend that word for the same mistake?
What specific behavior are you actually talking about?
distortions.reframeTemplate: The label I reached for was '______'. The accurate, specific version is: I did ______, once, in this situation. A mistake is something I made, not a name for who I am.
distortions.citation: Burns, D. D. (1980). Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy.

distortions.name: Personalization
distortions.description: You take responsibility for things that were not fully in your control, treating yourself as the cause of events that had many.
distortions.example: The team missed the target, and it is entirely my fault.
reframePrompts: What other factors and people shaped this outcome besides you?
What share of this was genuinely yours, honestly, as a percentage?
Are you confusing 'I was involved' with 'I caused all of it'?
distortions.reframeTemplate: I am carrying all of this as if it were mine alone. Realistically, my part was ______, and other factors were ______. I can own my share and put down the rest that was never mine to hold.
distortions.citation: Beck, A. T. (1979). Cognitive Therapy of Depression.
